claim: The mammalian cerebellum receives inputs from multiple sensory modalities.
source: The mammalian cerebellum is a highly multimodal structure, receiving inputs from multiple sensory modalities and integrating them during complex sensorimotor coordination tasks.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: Multimodal pathways converge onto individual cerebellar granule cells according to cell-type-specific anatomical projection mapping.
source: Previously, using cell-type-specific anatomical projection mapping, it was shown that multimodal pathways converge onto individual cerebellar granule cells (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2013.

claim: A subset of single granule cells receive convergent functional multimodal (somatosensory, auditory, and visual) inputs via separate mossy fibers.
source: Here we directly measure synaptic currents using in vivo patch-clamp recordings and confirm that a subset of single granule cells receive convergent functional multimodal (somatosensory, auditory, and visual) inputs via separate mossy fibers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on in vivo patch-clamp recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Integration of multimodal signals by granule cells can enhance action potential output.
source: Furthermore, we show that the integration of multimodal signals by granule cells can enhance action potential output.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The midbrain and cerebral association cortex integrate multimodal sensory signals.
source: Integrating multimodal sensory signals is one of the fundamental operations performed by the brain. The midbrain and cerebral association cortex (Stein and Stanford, 2008), and the cerebellum receive and process sensory signals of various modalities (Snider and Stowell, 1944; Azizi and Woodward, 1990; Gao et al., 1996; Sobel et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stein and Stanford, 2008.

claim: The cerebellum receives and processes sensory signals of various modalities.
source: Integrating multimodal sensory signals is one of the fundamental operations performed by the brain. The midbrain and cerebral association cortex (Stein and Stanford, 2008), and the cerebellum receive and process sensory signals of various modalities (Snider and Stowell, 1944; Azizi and Woodward, 1990; Gao et al., 1996; Sobel et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Snider and Stowell, 1944; Azizi and Woodward, 1990; Gao et al., 1996; Sobel et al., 1998.

claim: Each granule cell in the mammalian cerebellum receives excitatory synaptic inputs from on average four mossy fibers.
source: Although it is well known that each granule cell in the mammalian cerebellum receives excitatory synaptic inputs from on average four mossy fibers (Eccles et al., 1967; Jakab and Hamori, 1988), it is important to determine whether multisensory integration takes place already on the level of the granule cells, which form the input layer, or only in the downstream neurons, including Purkinje cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eccles et al., 1967 and Jakab and Hamori, 1988.

claim: Some granule cells receive mossy fibers from two areas in the brainstem (the basilar pontine nucleus and the external cuneate nucleus).
source: A recent study using projection mapping has shown that some granule cells receive mossy fibers from two areas in the brainstem (the basilar pontine nucleus and the external cuneate nucleus), providing morphological evidence of multimodal convergence in single granule cells (Huang et al., 2013; see also Chabrol et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2013 and Chabrol et al., 2015.

claim: In vivo single cerebellar granule cells in cats have been shown to only respond to stimulation of a single modality.
source: However, in vivo single cerebellar granule cells in cats have been shown to only respond to stimulation of a single modality (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006; Spanne and Jörntell, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006 and Spanne and Jörntell, 2015.

claim: 45% of granule cells (60/133 cells) in crus I and II responded to somatosensory stimulation with a burst of EPSCs.
source: 45% of granule cells (60/133 cells) in crus I and II and 10% of those (3/30 cells) in the dorsal paraflocculus responded to somatosensory stimulation with a burst of EPSCs (Figure 1A–E left column and Figure 1F–G), as described previously (Chadderton et al., 2004; Rancz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 10% of granule cells (3/30 cells) in the dorsal paraflocculus responded to somatosensory stimulation with a burst of EPSCs.
source: 45% of granule cells (60/133 cells) in crus I and II and 10% of those (3/30 cells) in the dorsal paraflocculus responded to somatosensory stimulation with a burst of EPSCs (Figure 1A–E left column and Figure 1F–G), as described previously (Chadderton et al., 2004; Rancz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Auditory stimulation (white noise, 81–91 dB SPL) evoked EPSCs in 25% of granule cells in crus I and II (33/133 cells).
source: In contrast, auditory stimulation (white noise, 81–91 dB SPL, Figure 1A–E middle column) evoked EPSCs in 25% of granule cells in crus I and II (33/133 cells) and 10% (3/30 cells) of granule cells in the dorsal paraflocculus (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Auditory stimulation evoked EPSCs in 10% (3/30 cells) of granule cells in the dorsal paraflocculus.
source: In contrast, auditory stimulation (white noise, 81–91 dB SPL, Figure 1A–E middle column) evoked EPSCs in 25% of granule cells in crus I and II (33/133 cells) and 10% (3/30 cells) of granule cells in the dorsal paraflocculus (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The number of evoked EPSC events increased with increasing sound levels (from 75 dB to 94 dB).
source: When different sound levels were systematically tested, the number of evoked EPSC events increased with increasing sound levels (from 75 dB to 94 dB), while the mean amplitude of evoked EPSCs remained constant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean amplitude of evoked EPSCs remained constant across different sound levels (from 75 dB to 94 dB).
source: When different sound levels were systematically tested, the number of evoked EPSC events increased with increasing sound levels (from 75 dB to 94 dB), while the mean amplitude of evoked EPSCs remained constant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Visual stimulation (binocular LED flash) evoked EPSCs in 87% of granule cells (26/30 cells) in the dorsal paraflocculus.
source: Finally, visual stimulation (binocular LED flash; Figure 1A–E right column) evoked EPSCs in 87% of granule cells (26/30 cells) in the dorsal paraflocculus, while visual responses in crus I and II were rare (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Visual responses in crus I and II were rare.
source: Finally, visual stimulation (binocular LED flash; Figure 1A–E right column) evoked EPSCs in 87% of granule cells (26/30 cells) in the dorsal paraflocculus, while visual responses in crus I and II were rare (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ipsilateral visual stimulation evoked the predominant response when visual stimulation was delivered monocularly.
source: When visual stimulation was delivered monocularly, ipsilateral stimulation evoked the predominant response (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Auditory and visual stimulation evoked bursts of EPSCs in granule cells that were comparable to those evoked by somatosensory stimulation.
source: In summary, auditory and visual stimulation evoked bursts of EPSCs in granule cells that were comparable to those evoked by somatosensory stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In dorsal paraflocculus 20% (6/30 cells) of granule cells were multisensory.
source: In dorsal paraflocculus 20% (6/30 cells) of granule cells were multisensory, and in crus I and II 14% (18/133 cells) were multisensory.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data.

claim: In crus I and II 14% (18/133 cells) of granule cells were multisensory.
source: In dorsal paraflocculus 20% (6/30 cells) of granule cells were multisensory, and in crus I and II 14% (18/133 cells) were multisensory.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data.

claim: Individual granule cells were found that responded to stimulation of three separate sensory modalities in both dorsal paraflocculus and crus I and II.
source: In both regions, we found individual granule cells that responded to stimulation of three separate sensory modalities.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data.

claim: The amplitude of auditory-evoked EPSCs (16.6 ± 0.8 pA, n = 23 sweeps) was significantly larger than that of somatosensory-evoked EPSCs (8.6 ± 1.2 pA, n = 23, P < 0.05) in the cell shown in Figure 2A–F.
source: In the cell shown in Figure 2A–F, the amplitude of auditory-evoked EPSCs (16.6 ± 0.8 pA, n = 23 sweeps) was significantly larger than that of somatosensory-evoked EPSCs (8.6 ± 1.2 pA, n = 23, P < 0.05), indicating that those two groups of EPSCs originate from different synapses, i.e. the signals are conveyed by different mossy fibers (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Different EPSC amplitudes in response to different modalities indicate that the signals are conveyed by different mossy fibers.
source: In the cell shown in Figure 2A–F, the amplitude of auditory-evoked EPSCs (16.6 ± 0.8 pA, n = 23 sweeps) was significantly larger than that of somatosensory-evoked EPSCs (8.6 ± 1.2 pA, n = 23, P < 0.05), indicating that those two groups of EPSCs originate from different synapses, i.e. the signals are conveyed by different mossy fibers (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the principle that EPSC amplitude and waveform reflect unique properties of distinct synapses.

claim: 40% (8/20) of multisensory cells showed significantly different (P < 0.05) first EPSC amplitudes in response to different modalities.
source: Across the population, 40% (8/20) of multisensory cells showed significantly different (P < 0.05) first EPSC amplitudes in response to different modalities (Figure 2G–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 2G–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: One cell showed a significant difference (P < 0.05) in EPSC rise time for the different modalities.
source: Additionally, one cell also showed a significant difference (P < 0.05) in EPSC rise time for the different modalities.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data.

claim: The linearity index showed considerable variation across cells and indicated moderately sublinear summation on average (0.71 ± 0.23; mean ± s.d.) for 8 cells that received inputs from two separate mossy fibers.
source: Interestingly, the linearity index showed considerable variation across cells and indicated moderately sublinear summation on average (0.71 ± 0.23; mean ± s.d.) for 8 cells that received inputs from two separate mossy fibers ( Figure 4C, see Discussion).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 4C.

claim: Cells that were not determined to have separate mossy fiber inputs for different modalities showed a linearity index of 0.70 ± 0.20 (mean ± s.d., n = 12).
source: The same tendency was seen for cells that were not determined to have separate mossy fiber inputs for different modalities (0.70 ± 0.20, mean ± s.d., n = 12), which was confirmed when the synaptic charge was used instead of event number to calculate the linearity index.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data.

claim: The resting membrane potential of granule cells was −55.0 ± 4.7 mV (n = 4).
source: The resting membrane potential and the action potential threshold were −55.0 ± 4.7 mV and −39.7 ± 3.0 mV (n = 4), respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from current-clamp recordings.

claim: The action potential threshold of granule cells was −39.7 ± 3.0 mV (n = 4).
source: The resting membrane potential and the action potential threshold were −55.0 ± 4.7 mV and −39.7 ± 3.0 mV (n = 4), respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from current-clamp recordings.

claim: Combined stimulation with two sensory modalities evoked more action potentials than the sum of two unimodal stimuli in the granule cell shown in Figure 3A–C, indicating supralinear summation.
source: In the granule cell shown in Figure 3A–C, combined stimulation with two sensory modalities evoked more action potentials than the sum of two unimodal stimuli, indicating supralinear summation.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Two of four cells exhibited supralinear summation of action potentials in response to combined sensory stimulation.
source: Two of four cells exhibited such supralinear summation (Cell 1 and 2 in Figure 3D), while the other two cells showed sublinear summation.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Two of four cells showed sublinear summation of action potentials in response to combined sensory stimulation.
source: Two of four cells exhibited such supralinear summation (Cell 1 and 2 in Figure 3D), while the other two cells showed sublinear summation.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Granule cells are capable of integrating multisensory signals to generate enhanced action potential output.
source: These findings suggest that, although there exists diversity across the population, granule cells are capable of integrating multisensory signals to generate enhanced action potential output.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing supralinear summation in some cells.

claim: Somatosensory inputs to crus I and II can be conveyed to individual granule cells by single mossy fibers.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have shown that somatosensory inputs to crus I and II (Chadderton et al., 2004; Rancz et al., 2007) and vestibular signals to the flocculus (Arenz et al., 2008) can be conveyed to individual granule cells by single mossy fibers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chadderton et al., 2004 and Rancz et al., 2007.

claim: Vestibular signals to the flocculus can be conveyed to individual granule cells by single mossy fibers.
source: Electrophysiological recordings have shown that somatosensory inputs to crus I and II (Chadderton et al., 2004; Rancz et al., 2007) and vestibular signals to the flocculus (Arenz et al., 2008) can be conveyed to individual granule cells by single mossy fibers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arenz et al., 2008.

claim: Single granule cells can receive mossy fibers of different origins according to anatomical and in vitro electrophysiological studies.
source: This conjecture has been supported by the recent anatomical (Huang et al., 2013) and in vitro electrophysiological (Chabrol et al., 2015) demonstration that single granule cells can receive mossy fibers of different origins (see also [Sawtell, 2010]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2013, Chabrol et al., 2015, and Sawtell, 2010.

claim: Combined stimulation of two sensory modalities can produce enhanced spike output from granule cells.
source: Furthermore, we show that combined stimulation of two sensory modalities can produce enhanced spike output from granule cells, indicating that the result of multisensory integration can be transmitted to downstream neurons in the cerebellar network.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The result of multisensory integration can be transmitted to downstream neurons in the cerebellar network.
source: Furthermore, we show that combined stimulation of two sensory modalities can produce enhanced spike output from granule cells, indicating that the result of multisensory integration can be transmitted to downstream neurons in the cerebellar network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multisensory integration enhances action potential output.

claim: The observed sublinear summation of synaptic currents is likely to be due to inhibitory interactions between the two sensory pathways upstream from the granule cell.
source: Under the excellent voltage-clamp conditions that exist in granule cells, inputs from different synapses are expected to summate linearly. Thus, the observed sublinear summation of synaptic currents is likely to be due to inhibitory interactions between the two sensory pathways upstream from the granule cell (see Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expectation of linear summation under good voltage-clamp conditions and the observation of sublinear summation.

claim: Inhibitory interactions between sensory pathways could occur at any point in upstream sensory pathways, including the brainstem, the thalamus and the cerebral cortex.
source: Such interactions could occur at any point in upstream sensory pathways, including the brainstem, the thalamus and the cerebral cortex, particularly given that the relatively long latency (> 10 ms) of sensory responses in our recordings suggests that these sensory signals are mediated via the corticocerebellar pathway rather than direct projections from primary sensory neurons (Morissette and Bower, 1996).
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms based on the observed data and cited literature.

claim: The relatively long latency (> 10 ms) of sensory responses suggests that these sensory signals are mediated via the corticocerebellar pathway rather than direct projections from primary sensory neurons.
source: Such interactions could occur at any point in upstream sensory pathways, including the brainstem, the thalamus and the cerebral cortex, particularly given that the relatively long latency (> 10 ms) of sensory responses in our recordings suggests that these sensory signals are mediated via the corticocerebellar pathway rather than direct projections from primary sensory neurons (Morissette and Bower, 1996).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed latency data and supported by citation to Morissette and Bower, 1996.

claim: Granule cells represent a diverse population with respect to functional multisensory input.
source: It is likely that granule cells represent a diverse population with respect to functional multisensory input (Figure 4), with some granule cells appearing to be unimodal, some with multisensory input delivered by separate mossy fibers, and some with multisensory input delivered by a single mossy fiber.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing different types of responses across the population.

claim: Some granule cells appear to be unimodal.
source: It is likely that granule cells represent a diverse population with respect to functional multisensory input (Figure 4), with some granule cells appearing to be unimodal, some with multisensory input delivered by separate mossy fibers, and some with multisensory input delivered by a single mossy fiber.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that not all granule cells responded to multiple modalities.

claim: Some granule cells have multisensory input delivered by separate mossy fibers.
source: It is likely that granule cells represent a diverse population with respect to functional multisensory input (Figure 4), with some granule cells appearing to be unimodal, some with multisensory input delivered by separate mossy fibers, and some with multisensory input delivered by a single mossy fiber.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing different EPSC amplitudes for different modalities in some cells.

claim: Some granule cells have multisensory input delivered by a single mossy fiber.
source: It is likely that granule cells represent a diverse population with respect to functional multisensory input (Figure 4), with some granule cells appearing to be unimodal, some with multisensory input delivered by separate mossy fibers, and some with multisensory input delivered by a single mossy fiber.
evidence: This is an inference based on cells that showed multisensory responses but did not have significantly different EPSC amplitudes.

claim: Influential theories of cerebellar computation have proposed that granule cells are not merely relaying signals but 'recoding' multiple types of incoming signals.
source: Indeed, influential theories of cerebellar computation (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971) have proposed that granule cells are not merely relaying signals but "recoding" multiple types of incoming signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marr, 1969 and Albus, 1971.

claim: The present study provides important in vivo functional evidence supporting the 'recoding' hypothesis in the mammalian cerebellum.
source: Our present study provides important in vivo functional evidence supporting this "recoding" hypothesis in the mammalian cerebellum.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: It was hypothesized that 'recoding' would expand the representation of population patterns because granule cells outnumber mossy fibers by a factor of 100 (due to the extensive branching of mossy fibers).
source: Moreover, it was hypothesized (Albus, 1971) that such "recoding" would expand the representation of population patterns because granule cells outnumber mossy fibers by a factor of 100 (due to the extensive branching of mossy fibers).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Albus, 1971.

claim: The linearity of summation (both in synaptic inputs and in spike outputs) varies across cells.
source: Our observation that the linearity of summation (both in synaptic inputs and in spike outputs) varies across cells may reflect the diversity of coding patterns required for the computational role of the granule cell in expansion recoding.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing variation in linearity indices across the population.

claim: The variation in linearity of summation may reflect the diversity of coding patterns required for the computational role of the granule cell in expansion recoding.
source: Our observation that the linearity of summation (both in synaptic inputs and in spike outputs) varies across cells may reflect the diversity of coding patterns required for the computational role of the granule cell in expansion recoding.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the observed variation.

claim: Synaptic plasticity at the mossy fiber-granule cell synapse may affect the representation of multiple sensory inputs at the level of a single granule cell.
source: In future studies, it will be important to reveal how synaptic plasticity at the mossy fiber-granule cell synapse (Roggeri et al., 2008) may affect the representation of multiple sensory inputs at the level of a single granule cell.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions, with citation to Roggeri et al., 2008 for synaptic plasticity.

claim: Patch-clamp recordings were made from granule cells in crus I and II and paraflocculus of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Whole cell voltage-clamp (V-C) and current-clamp (I-C) recordings were made from granule cells in crus I and II and paraflocculus of the cerebellar cortex, using a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Crus I and II and the dorsal paraflocculus were selected because previous studies suggested that these areas might receive multisensory inputs.
source: We selected crus I and II and the dorsal paraflocculus of the cerebellum because previous studies suggested that these areas might receive multisensory inputs (Azizi and Woodward, 1990; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on citations to Azizi and Woodward, 1990 and Huang et al., 2013.

claim: The high quality of voltage clamp recordings in granule cells in vivo enabled detection of individual sensory-evoked EPSCs.
source: The high quality of voltage clamp recordings in granule cells in vivo enabled detection of individual sensory-evoked EPSCs (Chadderton et al., 2004; Rancz et al., 2007; Arenz et al., 2008), thus providing exquisite sensitivity for detection of responses to a sensory stimulus.
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations to Chadderton et al., 2004; Rancz et al., 2007; Arenz et al., 2008.

claim: The amplitude and waveform of individual EPSCs reflect unique properties of distinct synapses.
source: To examine if responses to different sensory stimuli in a single granule cell were mediated by the same or separate mossy fibers, we analyzed the amplitude and waveform of individual EPSCs, since these characteristics reflect unique properties of distinct synapses (Silver et al., 1996; Arenz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Silver et al., 1996 and Arenz et al., 2008.

claim: For cells that did not exhibit a significant difference in EPSC amplitudes between modalities, it is not possible to determine if their multimodal input arises from a single mossy fiber or from two mossy fibers that have indistinguishable characteristics.
source: For the remaining cells that did not exhibit a significant difference in EPSC amplitudes between modalities, it is not possible to determine if their multimodal input arises from a single mossy fiber (Figure 4B) or from two mossy fibers that have indistinguishable characteristics (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a limitation of the analysis method acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Under excellent voltage-clamp conditions that exist in granule cells, inputs from different synapses are expected to summate linearly.
source: Under the excellent voltage-clamp conditions that exist in granule cells, inputs from different synapses are expected to summate linearly.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of voltage-clamp electrophysiology.

claim: The findings do not directly contradict the absence of multimodal integration observed in granule cells in decerebrate animals in which the corticocerebellar pathway is not preserved.
source: It should also be noted that our findings do not directly contradict the absence of multimodal integration observed in granule cells in decerebrate animals in which the corticocerebellar pathway is not preserved (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006; Spanne and Jörntell, 2015).
evidence: This is a discussion point reconciling the current findings with previous studies cited.

claim: Lister-hooded rats (19–24 days old) were used for experiments.
source: Lister-hooded rats (19–24 days old) were anaesthetized with a ketamine (60 mg/kg) and xylazine (4.5 mg/kg) mixture.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Rats were anaesthetized with a ketamine (60 mg/kg) and xylazine (4.5 mg/kg) mixture.
source: Lister-hooded rats (19–24 days old) were anaesthetized with a ketamine (60 mg/kg) and xylazine (4.5 mg/kg) mixture.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The estimated chloride reversal potential (ECl) was -69 mV with the internal solution used.
source: The internal solution contained: K-methanesulphonate 133 mM, KCl 7 mM, HEPES 10 mM, Mg-ATP 2 mM, Na2ATP 2 mM, Na2GTP 0.5 mM, EGTA 0.05 mM and biocytin 0.5%, pH 7.2, giving an estimated chloride reversal potential (ECl) of -69 mV.
evidence: This is a calculated value based on the internal solution composition.

claim: Voltage clamping at −70 mV allows excitatory synaptic currents to be observed in isolation.
source: This allows excitatory synaptic currents to be observed in isolation by voltage clamping at −70 mV.
evidence: This is based on the principle that voltage clamping near the chloride reversal potential isolates excitatory currents.
